title: Reading Logs and Getting a Shell
intro: These are the two commands you'll type more than any other in real life: logs and exec.

steps.explanation: By default this shows the current container's logs since it last started.

steps.fake_output:
2026-09-27 10:00:10 GET /health 200
2026-09-27 10:00:15 GET /api/users 200
(streaming... press Ctrl+C to stop)
steps.explanation: -f follows the log stream, just like tail -f on a regular file.

steps.prompt: The pod crashed and restarted. View the logs from BEFORE the crash.
steps.fake_output:
2026-09-27 09:58:40 ERROR: out of memory
2026-09-27 09:58:41 Container killed
steps.explanation: --previous shows the last terminated container's logs — essential for figuring out why something crashed, since the new container's logs won't show it.

steps.prompt: Get an interactive shell inside the pod.
steps.explanation: Useful for poking around live — checking env vars, testing DNS resolution, curling internal services. Not something to rely on for normal debugging though; logs/describe should usually be enough.
